item.title: Why You Shouldn’t Take Anything Personally
item.description:
Self-Help

Why You Shouldn’t Take Anything Personally

8 truths to help you stop absorbing other people's reactions.

Posted November 3, 2026

Key points
  • Other's judgements and reactions are influenced by their own experiences, insecurities, and emotional states.
  • Learning to observe rather than absorb other's behavior strengthens emotional regulation and resilience.
  • Taking accountability for our reactions includes recognizing that no one triggers you; you get triggered.
Source: Omar Lopez/Unsplash

Don’t take anything personally. Easier said than done. This represents the second agreement in the bestselling book The Four Agreements written by Don Miguel Ruiz (1997). In it, he astutely states, "Even when a situation seems so personal, even if others insult you directly, it has nothing to do with you. What they say, what they do, and the opinions they give are according to the agreements they have in their own minds."

Despite this, we find ourselves allowing someone's criticism, disapproval, or lack of responsiveness to determine how we feel about ourselves. Our mood and confidence can instantly shift because of a perceived disapproving tone or sensing that we’re the cause of someone’s irritation or frustration. We may react irrationally, impulsively, and intensely based on someone’s reactions, and our perceptions and interpretations.

Taking things personally is often an automatic psychological response shaped by our insecurities, attachment experiences, learned beliefs, and fundamental desire and need to belong. Research suggests that perceived rejection can activate our sympathetic nervous system, helping explain why interpersonal slights can feel disproportionately painful (Eisenberger et al., 2003).

8 truths that can build psychological flexibility to stop absorbing other people’s reactions

1. You do not like everyone; therefore, you cannot expect that everyone will like you.

Consider how many people you have encountered whom you did not particularly connect or resonate with. Sometimes we have negative feelings that get evoked solely by someone’s presence or mannerism, even if there isn’t any rational justification for it.

Our personal preferences are influenced by many factors such as another’s personality, values, expectations, etc. When we’re not readily accepted, or outwardly rejected, we assume and interpret it as evidence of our inadequacy or lack of worthiness.

Our brain’s tendency is to seek external approval and acceptance and gauge it as a valid measure of our worth. We’re taught this early on in our development and societal standards reinforce it. We frame it as: “If they think I have value, then I must. If they think I do not, then I must not.”

We do not learn that someone else’s preference or opinion is just that, and that our standards and opinion about ourselves matter most. You can reframe and consider that someone's preference for you doesn't determine your value, and you can be an incredible person, despite not being someone’s preferred person.

2. You cannot read minds. Your triggers, perceptions, judgments, and assumptions are all yours.

We frequently confuse our thoughts, feelings, and interpretations as absolute facts. If someone mistakenly doesn’t acknowledge us, we conclude that they don’t care about us and we’re not important enough to them. We also sometimes fail to own and take accountability for our own triggers and often get defensive, deflect, and blame to avoid facing our own fears and vulnerabilities.

In relationships, mind reading, personalization, catastrophizing, and other cognitive distortions can skew reality and be counterproductive and harmful (Beck, 2020). The inaccuracy is understandable given that our mind constructs explanations based on our past experiences, expectations, and emotional states.

To balance out your thinking, you can ask yourself: "What do I actually know, and what am I assuming? How else can I see this?" This is approaching the circumstance and person with overarching openness, curiosity, and expansiveness.

3. Criticism, aggression, and other harsh responses may reflect someone else's internal struggles.

Individuals can externalize their shame, frustration, insecurity, or unresolved emotional pain through hostility, defensiveness, or criticism. Psychodynamic theory describes projection as a defense mechanism through which individuals attribute aspects of their internal experience to others (Bailey & Pico 2023).

For example, a highly insecure person may be especially critical toward others. To distinguish whether a projection is being enacted, you can consider their delivery, intensity, or emotional reaction.

4. Negative energy is to be observed, not absorbed.

Imagine someone is speaking to you impatiently and with irritability. Within seconds, your chest tightens, your heart rate accelerates, your thoughts spiral, and you feel compelled to relent to protect yourself or actively defend yourself. Their emotional state has comingled and become yours.

Research on emotional contagion suggests that people can influence one another's emotional experiences, sometimes without conscious awareness (Wang, 2024). Self-awareness, self-regulation, and self-compassion don't require emotional absorption.

You can connect with and offer empathy for someone else’s reaction and experiences without absorbing and taking on their negative energy. It requires thoughtfully and mindfully deciphering what is theirs and what is yours, and how you choose to react to it.

5. Someone's negative mood is not automatically about you.

You may encounter distance, irritability enacted by a harsh tone or body language. Your immediate thought might be, "What did I do?" We often personalize others’ behavior, as connected to something we said or did, without evidence to support it.

Their mood can be reflective of their disappointment, fatigue, hormones, stress, or concerns that can be entirely unrelated to you. Before jumping to conclusions, approach with curiosity and consider asking, "I wonder if something’s going on for you. Is everything okay?" You can choose to approach with compassion and be attuned to someone's emotions without automatically assuming you're responsible for them.

6. Rejection doesn't define your worth.

Rejection can be particularly painful because belonging is a fundamental psychological need. Experiencing rejection can contribute to negative self-confidence, social anxiety, and the ability to sustain healthy trusting friendships and intimate relationships.

When someone rejects us, we often transform a specific experience into a more global conclusion. We make inferences such as “They didn’t choose me" becomes "I'm not good enough." Even though intellectually we know that rejection can reflect differing needs, incompatibility, timing, or circumstances beyond what we can control, we tend to personalize and generalize it.

You can remind yourself that your worth isn't determined by whether someone recognizes, attunes to, appreciates, or chooses you. You can’t avoid rejection, but you can strengthen your self-respect and self-compassion based on how you respond to it.

7. People's reactions provide you with vital information.

You can learn a lot from observing others’ reactions. It can give you a glimpse of their expectations, perspective, judgments, and emotional state. Emotional maturity involves vulnerability in noticing and acknowledging each person’s contribution, taking accountability, and repairing and healing when appropriate.

In order to accomplish this, you can identify if there is a difference of opinion, a divergent way of seeing circumstances, or an altered way of behaving based on differing core values. The goal is to evaluate, validate and reach mutual understanding so that future interactions can be healthier and more satisfying.

8. Proactively protect your emotional energy.

We can spend hours self-doubting, replaying conversations, anticipating rejection, questioning ourselves, or trying to change someone else's opinion of us. This rumination or perseveration spirals into thoughts about the thoughts, feelings about the feelings, thoughts about the feelings, and feelings about the thoughts. The emotional cost is exhaustion, exasperation, and typically extends beyond the original interaction.

Learning to notice, acknowledge, and interrupt your thoughts allows you to redirect your attention, even though your mind wants desperately to problem-solve. You could more readily focus on what you can directly influence, such as your interpretations, boundaries, responses, and choices.

The freedom of not making everything about you

The greatest emotional freedom comes when you no longer require other people to behave differently to feel secure within yourself. You recognize that you have choices regarding the way you respond.

You can recognize that you can be impacted by someone’s behavior without it defining you or automatically driving your behavior.

It can be challenging to notice parts of yourself that you would rather avoid or rid yourself of. Your activation, which can manifest itself as aggression, distancing, or in other ways, is about you. No one triggers you; you get triggered. Recognizing that can change not only how you experience others, but how you experience yourself.

item.title: Hard Times and the Practice of Staying Engaged
item.description:
Resilience

Hard Times and the Practice of Staying Engaged

Living with intention through a motto, a mantra, and a muse.

Posted November 3, 2026

Key points
  • Life’s difficulties can become opportunities for developing wisdom, creativity, and purpose.
  • The words we choose to live by can influence how we respond to uncertainty, resistance, and change.
  • Sources of inspiration, including memories, rituals, and relationships, can renew our sense of possibility.

Dedicated to Wendell Berry and The Berry Center, whose work continues to inspire care for the land, for community, and for the life we share.

In Standing by Words, Wendell Berry writes, “The impeded stream is the one that sings” (Berry, 1983). I keep returning to this line. Picture a stream running over a smooth, open bed. The water moves easily and makes almost no sound. Put stones in its path, and the water has to find its way around and over them, and that’s when we hear it. The resistance gives the stream its voice.

Berry’s image speaks to the way we live. He sees uncertainty, resistance, and inspiration as essential companions on any meaningful journey. Inspiration opens up possibility. When life becomes hard, our first instinct is usually to want the difficulty gone. We want certainty back. We want the stones out of the stream. Berry offers another way to see it: The moments of not knowing are where wisdom, creativity, and purpose take shape. The challenge is to stay engaged with what baffles and resists us long enough for it to shape us.

Guidance, Practice, and Renewal

A Motto, A Mantra, A Muse
Source: Dall-e / OpenAI

Staying engaged needs something to guide us, something to keep us practising, and something to renew us when we’re tired. In therapy, I talk about these as the three M’s of intentional living: a Motto, a Mantra, and a Muse. Each one answers one of Berry’s companions. A motto gives us direction when we’re uncertain. A mantra keeps us steady as we work through resistance. A muse inspires us and reminds us what’s possible.

The three M’s are personal, and the words people choose depend on what they’re facing. The following sections show how a motto, a mantra, and a muse take shape amid self-doubt, a strained relationship, and grief. These are struggles people commonly bring to therapy.

A Motto for Uncertainty

When we can’t see what lies ahead, we lose our bearings. A motto is a statement of principle that restores them, giving us a direction to walk in even as uncertainty remains.

For someone living with self-doubt, “My voice is worth hearing” affirms self-worth. When boundaries are strained, “I protect my peace” honours the right to inner calm. In grief, “I carry love forward” acknowledges the loss while embracing the love that remains. A good motto is short enough to remember and strong enough to stand up to doubt.

A Mantra for Resistance

Where the motto gives direction, the mantra sustains the practice. We meet resistance in the present moment, in the conversation we’re dreading or the morning that feels too heavy to begin. A mantra is the phrase we bring into those moments and repeat when we most need steadiness.

“I trust my own voice today” helps someone with self-doubt speak up. “I honour my limits with kindness” affirms self-respect without hostility. “I carry their love in my heart” becomes a daily act of remembrance. Each repetition strengthens conviction, and over time the mantra becomes part of the inner language that steadies us. This is the impeded stream finding its way, one stone at a time.

A Muse for Inspiration

A muse is our source of inspiration. It’s often found in a memory, a ritual, or a symbol: a teacher who encouraged us, a practice that restores balance, a place that brings rest.

In self-doubt, a muse might be the memory of being supported. When strengthening boundaries, it might be a place, real or remembered, that offers safety. In grief, a family ritual, a piece of music or a well-worn object can become a bridge between what was and what continues.

Choosing the Words

The words that steady us rarely emerge fully formed but slowly surface through reflection, often by noticing what we already value and naming it. The questions below are some I’ve found helpful in therapy for drawing out a motto, a mantra, and a muse. Each answer is personal, reflecting something of our experience and what rings true for us.

Motto: Clarifying what matters most

A statement of principle that guides and steadies us through uncertainty.

The motto questions open a reflective space about values, principles, and direction:

  1. “When life feels uncertain or challenging, what words would remind you of what truly matters to you?”
  2. “If you were to name a guiding truth or principle that could help you stay anchored during difficult times, what might it be?”
  3. “What brief phrase could capture the kind of person you hope to be, even when things feel unclear or hard?”

Mantra: Strengthening the practice of living

A phrase repeated in the present moment to cultivate steadiness and self-trust.

The mantra questions help people experiment with language that soothes, empowers, and motivates:

  1. “What simple, supportive words could you gently repeat to yourself when you need strength or reassurance?”
  2. “If you could speak one small reminder to yourself each day to help you move toward the life you want, what might it sound like?”
  3. “How might you express your guiding principle in a way that you could return to—again and again—when you need grounding?”

Muse: Reconnecting with inspiration and possibility

A source of renewal that stirs imagination and reminds us of what gives life meaning.

The muse questions explore the deeper wells of memory, imagination, and inspiration that sustain growth:

  1. “Who or what in your life has helped you remember what is possible, even in difficult times?”
  2. “Is there a place, memory, story, or symbol that reconnects you with hope, strength, or a sense of meaning?”
  3. “When you picture the best in yourself, or the life you wish to grow into, what image, experience, or influence comes to mind?”

Our Deepest Form

People I see in therapy often describe this work as grounding, clarifying, and connecting, because it links inner reflection with outward action.

We all go through seasons when our confidence dips, when relationships test us, or when we feel the weight of grief. Berry’s insight is that these are the seasons when our lives take their deepest form. A motto, a mantra, and a muse help us move through them with intention. They keep us engaged with what unsettles and resists us, so we can learn what those difficulties have to teach. Like Berry’s stream, we find our voice by meeting what stands in our way.

item.title: Is Love For Dogs Always "A Many Splendored Thing?"
item.description:
Animal Behavior

Is Love For Dogs Always "A Many Splendored Thing?"

A recent book explains the many complicated sides of canine love.

Posted November 3, 2026

Key points
  • Caring for animals requires us to look beyond sentiment and think about consequences of the relationship.
  • It's essential for us to take the dogs point of view in so-called loving relationships.
  • Why do so many dogs ask in bewilderment of their human, "Do you love me or love me not?"
Source: Anil Sharma/Pexels.

I know I'm not alone to have experienced people say something like, "I love my dog" and then observe countless different sorts of human-dog relationships that can change in the blink of an eye. I'm not saying that the people who claim they love their dog don't, but in many cases when they tell me that and I see how they mistreat their canine companion I can only say, "I glad they don't love me."

I've always wanted to know more about the variegated nature of human-dog relationships and was pleased to learn of Melina Jacques' recent book What It Really Means To Love Dogs: A Cultural And Ethical Exploration in which she discusses "a set of contradictions that are widely experienced but rarely named. Certain forms of intrusion become routine, while those expected to accommodate them are often left without a clear way to articulate what is happening."

Marc Bekoff: What are some of the topics you consider and what are some of your major messages?

Melina Jacques: One of the book’s central arguments is that dogs have become powerful cultural symbols associated with goodness, compassion, love, loyalty, and virtue. A significant portion of the book explores how this symbolic status emerged and why it is so vigorously defended.

The book examines how this symbolic status influences public attitudes toward dogs and can discourage critical discussion of issues that would be readily and openly addressed in other contexts. It explores the consequences of dog ownership for human communities, including attacks, chronic noise, neighbourhood conflict, relationship breakdown, and the diversion of resources and attention away from other priorities. For example, dog attacks in the United States result in reconstructive surgery approximately every 19 minutes, with children disproportionately represented among the victims. Yet discussions of dog attacks are often redirected toward individual circumstances or responsible ownership rather than examining broader questions about the normalization of dog ownership and public safety.

Source: Melina Jacques

Persistent barking can have consequences far beyond sleep deprivation. Repeated exposure to unwanted, unpredictable noise can activate the body’s physiological stress-response systems, involving stress hormones such as cortisol and adrenaline. Over time, chronic noise exposure can contribute to sustained psychological distress and adverse cardiovascular and metabolic health effects, effectively making people’s own homes sources of chronic environmental stress.

article continues after advertisement

Conflicts over dogs' behaviour and the prioritization of dogs' needs can also contribute to tension and relationship breakdown. These are not simply isolated inconveniences but consequences of a cultural environment in which the presence and interests of dogs are often treated as beyond question. Municipalities also devote resources to animal shelters and responding to complaints and attacks.

I also examine the ecological impacts of dogs, including predation, disease transmission, disturbance of wildlife, nutrient pollution, and threats to vulnerable species. Research discussed in the book implicates dogs in 11 vertebrate extinctions and identifies nearly 200 species worldwide that are threatened by their impacts.

These impacts extend beyond direct predation. The scent of dog urine, for example, can alter wildlife behaviour, causing wild animals to avoid otherwise suitable and valuable habitat. Dog waste also introduces nutrients into the environment, contributing to nutrient pollution and affecting surrounding ecosystems. Dogs can also introduce infectious diseases and parasites into wildlife populations. Free-ranging dogs, in particular, can act as reservoirs or sources of transmission for pathogens, such as parvovirus or canine distemper, that affect wild carnivores and other susceptible species, sometimes placing additional pressure on already vulnerable populations.

Hybridization presents another ecological concern. Domestic dogs can interbreed with wild canids, including grey wolves and golden jackals, introducing domestic-dog genes into wild populations and potentially compromising their genetic integrity.

Another major theme concerns dogs themselves. Although dogs are widely regarded as among the most loved animals on Earth, I question whether many aspects of modern dog ownership truly serve their interests. For example, breeding dogs to satisfy human preferences for particular physical characteristics can produce animals with serious inherited health problems, raising questions about whether commercial interests and aesthetic preferences are being prioritized over dogs’ physical well-being and quality of life.

Similarly, behaviours that may reflect frustration or unmet needs arising from unsuitable living conditions are increasingly being managed with psychotropic medications. Rather than addressing the underlying circumstances contributing to dogs’ distress, we may simply be medicating behaviours that humans find inconvenient or undesirable.

article continues after advertisement

The book also explores the economic and psychological forces that sustain dog culture, including the role of the pet industry, social incentives, identity, and moral self-image. The pet industry, for example, has developed an enormous commercial ecosystem around dog ownership, encompassing food, accessories, grooming, training, veterinary services, insurance, and other products and services. These commercial interests benefit from the normalization and expansion of dog ownership.

At the psychological level, dog ownership can also become intertwined with personal identity and moral self-image. People may regard owning or adopting a dog as evidence of their compassion and kindness, making criticism of dog-related practices feel like a personal attack rather than an opportunity to examine the consequences of those practices. The book explores how these economic interests and cultural beliefs reinforce one another, helping to sustain a culture that is rarely subjected to critical scrutiny.

At its broadest level, the book asks a simple question: What does it actually mean to love a dog? My conclusion is that caring responsibly for animals requires us to look beyond sentiment and think honestly about the consequences of the relationships we create with animals.

MB: How does your book differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

MJ: Many books explore dogs through the lenses of behaviour, cognition, welfare, history, or companionship. My book differs in that it places these topics within a larger examination of dog culture itself and the consequences that arise from it.

Rather than treating dogs solely as animals, I examine them as cultural symbols and explore how that symbolic status shapes public attitudes, social norms, and policy decisions. The book also investigates an institution that is rarely subjected to critical scrutiny: pet ownership itself.

article continues after advertisement

Drawing on multiple disciplines, it investigates why dogs occupy such a unique place in human society and what consequences follow from that distinction.

MB: Are you hopeful that as people learn more about what it really means to love a dog they will give their companion canine a better and more fulfilled life, a win-win for all?

MJ: Yes, although perhaps not in exactly that way. If readers come away with a deeper understanding of dogs and a greater willingness to think critically about their needs, many dogs could benefit. One of the book’s central themes is that genuine concern for dogs requires us to ask whether the lives we create for them are truly compatible with their interests.

At the same time, I hope readers expand their circle of concern beyond individual dogs to include human communities, wildlife, ecosystems, and other animals affected by our relationship with dogs. If the book encourages people to reflect more deeply on those questions, I would consider that a positive outcome.

item.title: Early Medical Pain Can Produce a Lasting Memory
item.description:
Epigenetics

Early Medical Pain Can Produce a Lasting Memory

Painful procedures in infancy and childhood may leave lasting epigenetic marks.

Posted November 3, 2026

Key points
  • Newborns feel pain, and pain early in life can change how the nervous system responds to pain later.
  • Epigenetic changes may help explain how early experiences affect us later in life.
  • Pain relief and comfort during medical procedures early in life may reduce the effects of harm later in life.

Several years ago, I worked with a woman who experienced trauma on the first day of her life. She was born with Rh incompatibility, a potentially deadly condition that occurs when an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive baby and her immune system attacks the baby's red blood cells. This woman required a blood transfusion in which all of the blood in her body was drained and was replaced with transfused blood. This medical procedure saved her life, but she is experiencing lasting psychological adverse effects from the trauma associated with this procedure.

As a medical student, I remember watching an infant with his arms and legs strapped down to a board in order for the doctor to perform a circumcision. As the baby cried and screamed, the doctor performing the procedure said that the young boy would not remember this procedure years later. No anesthesia was used. Was the doctor correct? I have wondered about this for more than 40 years, and I can tell you that my research into epigenetic memory has taught me that he was probably wrong.

As a father, I took my 2-year-old daughter to a routine pediatrician's appointment for a vaccination. She cried after the shot, but otherwise seemed OK. The doctor told us she would probably have a sore leg the next day, but Tylenol would take care of it. Well, the next day, our daughter wouldn't walk on her sore leg. She cried and cried, despite our efforts to manage her pain with Tylenol and Ibuprofen. Well, years later, our daughter grew up to be one of the most courageous women I know. She climbed every 14,000-foot mountain in Colorado—all 58 of them! But she has had to deal with a lifelong fear of needles. If she has blood drawn, she has to lie down because she is likely to pass out if she sees the needle. For years, I have wondered: Is her fear of needles related to that early vaccination?

What Does the Research Say?

Babies can experience pain
Source: Antoni Shkraba / Pexels

For much of the 20th century, physicians believed that newborns didn’t feel pain. Infants commonly underwent surgery with little or no anesthesia. That belief began to change in 1987, when a review published in The New England Journal of Medicine showed that newborns can experience pain, and they can also experience powerful stress responses due to the pain.

This raises the question: Can pain experienced early in life create a memory that persists for years? Research involving epigenetic memory suggests it is possible.

What Is Epigenetic Memory?

Epigenetics refers to chemical modifications that alter how genes are expressed without changing the DNA sequence. These modifications help cells “remember” what has previously happened.

In 2004, a study in Nature Neuroscience showed that rat pups receiving little maternal care developed epigenetic modifications to a gene in the hippocampus that left them with exaggerated stress responses as adults. Five years later, another study found similar changes in the brains of suicide victims who had been abused as children. These studies suggested that early trauma can be remembered by modifications to our cells’ DNA.

Pain in the Newborn Intensive Care Unit

Baby in ICU
Source: Yobro10 / iStock

Strong evidence in humans linking medical procedures to epigenetic change comes from studies involving premature infants. These babies may undergo about 10 painful procedures per day, including heel lances, needle sticks, intubation, and suctioning.

An Italian study found that very preterm infants exposed to more skin-breaking procedures showed increased changes to the serotonin transporter gene between birth and discharge. Serotonin helps regulate mood, anxiety, and pain. A follow-up study linked these changes to greater negative emotionality at 3 months of age.

These changes may persist. Researchers in Canada found that at age 7, children born very preterm had greater epigenetic changes than full-term peers. Neonatal pain predicted that epigenetic changes were associated with more behavior problems later in life. This same group later connected greater neonatal procedural pain to physical changes in the brains of these children at the age of 8.

Circumcision

Healthy, full-term infants are not immune to these trauma-induced changes. Newborn circumcision is one of the most common surgical procedures performed in the United States, and historically it was often done without anesthesia.

In a 1995 study, researchers noticed that circumcised boys cried longer and showed more pain behavior during vaccinations at 4 to 6 months of age than uncircumcised boys. Their prospective 1997 study confirmed it. Circumcised infants reacted more strongly to routine vaccination months later than those who had received a topical anesthetic before circumcision.

In other words, a single painful event in the first days of life appeared to change the infant’s pain system, and pain relief partly prevented it. Whether epigenetic changes underlie this effect has not been directly tested, but the pattern of lasting sensitization from early pain fits closely with the previously described findings.

Older Children

Toddlers and school-age children remember procedures as well. A review found that a minority of children develop posttraumatic stress symptoms after surgery, and 12 to 31 percent of children undergoing cardiac surgery develop posttraumatic stress disorder. Medical fear in childhood can also shape how people approach health care as adults.

The evidence is preliminary that these changes are due to epigenetic memory. But it is encouraging to note that epigenetic changes appear to be potentially reversible, and maternal sensitivity can reduce these effects in full-term infants.

What This Means for Parents and Clinicians

Skin-to-skin contact can reduce trauma
Source: Alamin Hossain / Pexels

Necessary procedures should not be avoided because of fear. But the evidence argues that we should be taking infant and child pain seriously. Strategies for reducing the effects of painful and other traumatic procedures include providing anesthesia for circumcision and analgesia for other painful procedures, offering skin-to-skin contact, or breastfeeding during needle sticks, avoiding unnecessary procedures, and preparing older children for what to expect.

The infant may not remember the procedure. But their body may.

item.title: How to End the Year with Purpose
item.description:
Productivity

How to End the Year with Purpose

Author Tiago Forte on finding clarity and direction in the 'Annual Life Review.'

Posted November 3, 2026

As the year winds down, we can find ourselves consumed with the busyness of the holiday season, in the thick of responsibility at work and school, and perhaps wondering if we are just spinning our wheels, glancing back to see where the time has gone.

For productivity expert and author Tiago Forte, the Annual Life Review has become an anchor in his yearly rhythm, providing clarity and direction for a life lived with intention. Grab a journal and a pen, a copy of Forte’s latest book, Life in Perspective: The Art and Power of the Annual Life Review, and make deep self-reflection a gift you give to yourself each year.

Author and productivity expert Tiago Forte shares the secret to ending the year strong with an Annual Life Review in his latest book, "Life in Perspective."
Source: Lauren Valdez/Used with permission

Q: Share a bit about your background and what inspired you to write Life in Perspective.

Tiago Forte: I've been a content creator, coach, teacher, and author for the last 13 years, focused on helping people become more productive with technology. I decided to write this book because I realized over those years that being productive is not helpful if you don't have a clear sense of where you're going and why.

Modern technology is an incredibly powerful force for getting what you want, but you have to know what you truly want in the first place; otherwise it will just fill your time with distraction and noise. My personal answer to this need for deeper intention has been a practice called the Annual Life Review, which I've followed every year for the last 17 years, and this book is my attempt to make it available to others who feel the same need for clarity and balance in our rapidly changing world.

Q: How has practicing an annual life review impacted your own life? In today’s fast-paced world where many of us are seeking answers online, what is the value of looking within for the validation, direction, and inspiration we need?

Tiago Forte: There are endless sources of external information that we're flooded with every day, all year long: podcasts and videos we consume, the advice of gurus and media personalities, and the digital feeds that seek to dominate our attention on every platform.

The annual life review is about turning down the volume on all those external sources and tuning in to internal ones instead – our inner voice, our intuition, our desires, our dreams. No one else can tell us what is right for us, in our unique life circumstances, or what we need to feel fulfilled and joyful. The only source for those kinds of answers lies inside.

The benefit of finding those answers, which I've experienced again and again, is a sense of deep calm, peace, certainty, and self-confidence that I know where my life and career are headed.

Q: What is the method that you disseminate in this book, and how can readers apply it to their own reflective practice?

Tiago Forte: When I first started conducting annual reviews, there was no method or framework to help me structure them. So my process was haphazard and filled with mistakes and wrong turns. Later on, when I learned that many others also practiced year-end reviews of some kind, there was still no definitive book or method to follow.

Annual Review Course (ARC) is the one I developed over the years, first for myself, and later for the students in my course. It takes you on a learning journey from the past, through the present, and finally to the future, where all the insights and realizations you gleaned from the past and present can inform your future plans.

Q: What role might reading and journaling play in this process of annual life review? How have reading and writing helped you to grow, personally?

Tiago Forte: Reading and journaling play a crucial role in the annual review, alongside many of the most proven practices that many people are already familiar with, like meditation, reflection in nature, visualization, and goal-setting.

What the annual life review does is place all those practices into a framework so they build and compound on each other. This leads to an experience that is more than the sum of its parts – a crescendo of insight and meaning that no single one can produce on its own.

Source: Simon and Schuster/Used with permission

Q: How do you hope Life in Perspective changes readers’ lives for the better?

Tiago Forte: I hope it gives them a counterbalance to the fear, uncertainty, chaos, and mental fragmentation that modern life often creates in our lives. A special time and place that they know they can set aside once per year, or anytime they want to return to themselves, and reliably reach a state of balance and clarity. I hope it introduces them to a wider global community of reviewers, from whom they can learn and be inspired. I hope it becomes a cornerstone of their self-reflection and provides a foundation of intention for years to come.

item.title: 3 Steps to De-Catastrophize Your Anxious Thoughts
item.description:
Catastrophizing

3 Steps to De-Catastrophize Your Anxious Thoughts

De-escalating your "big feelings" begins with taking three small steps.

Posted November 3, 2026

Source: Ruslan Rozanov / Pexels

People with anxiety often come to therapy complaining of a specific and extreme form of worrying. They ask questions like:

  • “If my partner does not reply to me the second I text them, I always assume that the worst might have happened. How do I manage this habit?”
  • “I cannot stand the thought of failing my exam; it makes me feel like I will always be a failure in life. Is this normal?”
  • Whenever I meet someone new, even the slightest weird signal from them makes me think they hate me. How can I break this destructive habit?”

If your mind also plays a reel of worst-case scenarios every time your anxiety rises, you might be engaging in catastrophizing. Catastrophic thinking is distorted perception and cognition.

Typically, when a person catastrophizes, they blow things out of proportion and feel irrationally threatened by current, past, or imaginary situations. If you tend to catastrophize, here are three steps to de-escalate your thought processes.

1. Come back to the present

Catastrophizing can quickly lead you down a dark thought spiral. The best thing to do: Immediately bring yourself back to the present.

Research published in Acta Psychologica suggests that mindfulness, both in the moment and as a personality trait, shows great promise as a combatant to anxiety and catastrophizing. Training and practicing mindfulness can give your emotion regulation faculties a much-needed boost.

Another practice that can help someone who struggles with catastrophizing is breathwork. Research shows that deep breathing — or diaphragmatic breathing — relieves anxiety by lowering heart rate and blood pressure. Focusing on your breath grounds you in the present and therefore acts as a buffer between you and your catastrophic thoughts.

2. Establish a worrying time

Small worries accumulate and turn into catastrophic thinking. Research explains that setting aside and scheduling a block of time solely for worrying is a simple but effective stress-management technique.

If you have anxious or catastrophic thoughts during an important moment, defer them to your ‘worry time’ and focus on the present moment. It can also help you become aware of and address your anxieties.

3. Give CBT a shot

Since catastrophizing is a cognitive distortion or, simply put, a malfunctioning thought process, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is recommended most often when it comes to addressing catastrophic thinking.

Research shows CBT is effective against catastrophizing; it is based on awareness. Under CBT, the person struggling with catastrophizing is made aware of the dysfunction in emotion regulation and thought processes and is given exercises tailored to dismantle irrational thinking.

Often, the best antidote to catastrophic thinking is to talk to someone who can offer an objective perspective, like a therapist or counselor.

As with other distorted thought processes, catastrophizing flourishes in isolation. The first thing anyone should do when they can’t control their own disturbing thoughts is to say them out loud, preferably to a loved one or a medical professional.
